extracted.intended_audience: Canadian patent practitioners, applicants, patent examiners, and IP counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal/practice criteria for determining whether claimed subject-matter is patent-eligible in Canada, focusing on statutory categories, judicial exclusions (abstract ideas), the CIPO 'actual invention' approach, and the role of synergy/aggregation in segregating claim parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory categories of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent-eligible subject-matter must fall within one of the statutory categories listed in the Patent Act definition of 'invention': art, process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim that does not fall within one of these categories fails the threshold question of patent-eligibility under the Patent Act. This is the starting point for eligibility analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract ideas prohibition (subsection 27(8))
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Act contains a categorical exclusion: 'no patent shall be granted for any mere scientific principle or abstract theorem'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have interpreted this to encompass calculations and mathematical formulae per se, mental operations and processes, plans or information transformations involving no change to underlying physical entities, schemes or rules (including games) that use conventional equipment, and computer programs per se. A disembodied idea is not patent-eligible; only practical applications may be.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physicality / discernible effect requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject-matter is generally patent-eligible if, when performed or employed, it involves some physical existence or manifestation of a discernible effect or change ('physicality').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, merely performing patent-ineligible subject-matter (e.g., an abstract algorithm) on a physical computing device does not, without more, render the subject-matter patent-eligible. The physical manifestation must meaningfully contribute to the invention's character as a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of the 'actual invention' (CIPO current guidelines)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'actual invention' is identified as either a single element or a combination of elements that provide a solution to a problem; the claim must be limited to or narrower than an actual invention that meets the physicality standard and relates to the manual or productive arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elements that are essential in the applicant's intention but have no material effect on the working of the 'actual invention' (superfluous limitations) may not form part of the 'actual invention'. The requirement that a claim be limited to or narrower than an actual invention means the claim must place the fences around the entirety of an actual invention or some part of an actual invention; claims that fence subject-matter not part of an actual invention may fail subsection 27(4) clarity requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted segregation of claimed subject-matter into parts (where warranted)
rubrics_metrics.description: The current guidelines allow segregation of claimed subject-matter into parts when those parts do not cooperate together to produce the solution (i.e., where there is no synergy), permitting assessment of those parts separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice aligns with existing patentability doctrines (e.g., distinction between patentable combinations and mere aggregations) and MOPOP guidance that allows considering parts separately in cases of mere aggregations. It contrasts with earlier (invalidated) guidelines that isolated only the inventive contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable combination vs mere aggregation (synergy test)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentable combination is where elements cooperate together to produce a unitary new or unexpected result; a mere aggregation is a juxtaposition of known parts each functioning as expected without producing a combined synergistic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Synergy (interaction producing a total effect greater than the sum of individual elements) is the key; where elements form a true combination, all elements must be considered as a whole for eligibility and judicial exclusions. Where only an aggregation exists, individual parts can be assessed separately for novelty/obviousness (and may be obvious). MOPOP: 'An aggregation of old parts cannot form the basis of a patentable invention.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of segregating to 'inventive contribution' alone
rubrics_metrics.description: Previous CIPO practice that segregated and assessed only the 'inventive contribution' (the combination of claim elements not taught by prior art) was invalidated by courts because the proper object of assessment is 'the subject matter defined by the claim' rather than an inventor's characterization of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners and practitioners should not isolate only the novel elements and ignore the claim as defined; the claim must be assessed consistent with case law (see Re Amazon.com Inc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: MOPOP guidance on considering essential elements that cooperate
rubrics_metrics.description: In identifying the actual invention, it is appropriate to consider solutions evident to a person skilled in the art on reading the specification, and the actual invention must consider all essential elements (as purposively construed) that cooperate together to achieve the solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For claims with a single essential element, analysis focuses on whether that element achieves the solution; for claims with multiple essential elements, analysis must consider any combination of those elements that cooperate to achieve the solution. The actual invention is not necessarily limited to the inventive aspect alone and may include known elements that cooperate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhaustive combination and claim clarity (subsection 27(4) interaction)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim must place the fences properly around the actual invention or part thereof; claims that define subject-matter beyond the immediate and cooperating environment of the invention ('exhaustive combinations') may be rejected for lack of clarity (subsection 27(4)) or unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practically, examiners sometimes raise unity-style objections under subsection 27(4) for claims that contain multiple inventive concepts or where the inventive concept is unclear. MOPOP references (e.g., 16.07.01 and 21.07.01) address related examiner practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of mere aggregations under obviousness (section 28.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere aggregations should be identified as a defect under section 28.3 of the Patent Act as being obvious; separate prior art documents may be cited to show that each individual part is known in the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where claimed subject-matter is a mere aggregation, the examiner can rely on multiple prior art sources to show each element was known and thus render the claim obvious. This shows how patentability (novelty/obviousness) of parts can be assessed separately where there is no synergy.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPIC Framework for computer-implemented inventions (three-step approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: IPIC proposed framework (included by court order in Benjamin Moore) directs examiners to: purposively construe the claim; ask whether the construed claim as a whole is only a mere scientific principle/abstract theorem or comprises a practical application employing such a principle; if practical, assess the construed claim for remaining patentability criteria (statutory categories, judicial exclusions) and for novelty, obviousness and utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This framework emphasizes assessing the claim as a whole first (purposive construction) and only if the claim is a practical application should further patentability assessments be performed. The Federal Court included the IPIC Framework in its Order for reassessment of particular applications, and its status is subject to appeal at the Federal Court of Appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of known elements within 'actual invention'
rubrics_metrics.description: The current guidelines explicitly permit that known elements may form part of an 'actual invention' if they cooperate with other elements to achieve the solution; the actual invention 'will not necessarily be limited to the element or elements that constitute the inventive aspect'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should not assume that only newly-contributed matter can constitute the actual invention; assess whether known elements are essential to the cooperative combination producing the solution.
